Question nine. What are type one and type two errors, and what is power? Type one is a false positive, rejecting a true null, at rate alpha. Type two is a false negative, missing a real effect, at rate beta. Power, one minus beta, is the chance of catching a real effect. It rises with more data, a bigger effect, less noise, or a looser alpha. Lowering alpha trades false positives for false negatives. Whether users notice is an online test, where you choose the sample size. Catching a click rate moving from five percent to five and a half, at eighty percent power, takes about thirty-one thousand users per arm. Half that lift takes four times the users. With five thousand per arm, that lift is caught one time in five. So a test that small, which finds nothing, hasn't shown the models are equal. Every test so far trusted the sample. Next, whether it's the right one.

Question ten. What is selection bias? The sample doesn't represent the population you want to generalize to, so estimates stay off however much data you collect. In machine learning, it's training on a population unlike your serving traffic. In a simulation, a lender only sees defaults on the loans it approved. Among those, five point three percent default. Across every applicant, it's eleven point six percent. Sixty times as many approved loans don't close that gap. The fix is in how the data is collected. Approve a small random slice whatever the score, here two percent, and its default rate is eleven point eight percent. The price is some bad loans, for labels you can trust.
